after: ## Why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain
alt: Six factors surround the Industrial Revolution in Britain, about 1760 to 1840: resources, agricultural change, capital from trade, markets and empire, transport, and political stability.
caption: Several factors worked together; strong answers show how they link.

alt: A vertical timeline: Darby smelts iron with coke (1709), Newcomen’s steam engine (1712), Kay’s flying shuttle (1733), the Bridgewater Canal (1761), the spinning jenny (about 1764), Arkwright’s water frame and Watt’s separate condenser (1769), Crompton’s mule (1779), Cartwright’s power loom (1785), the Stockton and Darlington Railway (1825) and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830), colour-coded as power, textiles or transport.
caption: Get the dates right: Newcomen’s engine (1712) came long before Watt’s condenser (1769).

alt: Left: a loop in which faster weaving raises demand for yarn, spinning is mechanised, and faster weaving is needed again. Right: a chain in which machines need power, water gives way to steam, steam needs coal, and coal needs better transport.
caption: Each invention created the problem the next one solved.

alt: A timeline of when industrialisation took off: Britain about 1760, the USA after the Civil War, Japan after the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Germany after unification in 1871, the USSR with Five-Year Plans from 1928, the East Asian economies from the 1960s and China with reforms from 1978.
caption: Later starters borrowed technology and relied on the state, so they moved faster.

alt: Work moved from the domestic putting-out system to factories run by clock and machine for 12 to 14 hours a day. Responses included the Luddites, growing trade unions and the Chartists. Reform followed slowly with the Factory Act of 1833 and the Mines Act of 1842.
caption: Factory work provoked protest and organisation before reform slowly followed.

alt: Bars for fictional Harrowby: 12,000 people in 1801, 39,000 in 1831 and 96,000 in 1861. Growth was 225% (27,000 people) from 1801 to 1831 and 146.2% (57,000 people) from 1831 to 1861; overall it was 700%, an eightfold rise.
caption: Percentage growth fell after 1831 while the number of extra people rose: say which measure you mean.

alt: Stacked bars for fictional Norland. In 1800 jobs were 62% primary, 22% secondary and 16% tertiary; in 1900, 18%, 46% and 36%; in 2020, 2%, 17% and 81%. Secondary rose 24 percentage points then fell 29, while tertiary rose 45 points after 1900.
caption: Manufacturing rose then fell as services took over: measure the change in percentage points.

alt: Six steps for a criterion B plan: a focused research question such as how far the 1833 Factory Act improved conditions for child workers, a justification, a method using primary and secondary sources, a dated action plan, consistent recording and referencing, and an evaluation.
caption: Six steps take a plan from a focused question to an honest evaluation.
